messages.content: Explain how DNS caching works to a new software developer in 17 short sentences.

message.content:
DNS translates human-readable domain names into machine-readable IP addresses.
Every time you visit a site, your computer asks a DNS resolver for this mapping.
Caching stores these results temporarily to avoid repeating the lookup process.
Your operating system checks its local cache first for any known records.
If missing, the request moves to your browser's internal DNS cache.
Browsers often keep recent lookups for a few seconds to speed up navigation.
Your ISP or public DNS provider maintains a larger, shared cache server.
This intermediate server remembers queries from many users across the network.
Each DNS record has a specific duration called Time To Live, or TTL.
The TTL dictates how long a cached entry remains valid before expiring.
When a cache entry expires, the system must perform a fresh lookup again.
This hierarchy reduces traffic on the root and authoritative name servers.
Faster resolution times improve the overall user experience significantly.
However, stale data can cause issues if a server IP changes unexpectedly.
Developers must manage TTL values carefully during deployments or migrations.
You can manually flush your local cache if you suspect incorrect data.
Understanding these layers helps you debug connectivity problems effectively.
